newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs challenge Lamfalussy on unemployment.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs challenge Lamfalussy on unemployment.

text.p: The European Parliament told European Monetary Institute (EMI) chief Alexander Lamfalussy on Tuesday that economic and monetary union (EMU) would not keep public support unless it helped reduce unemployment.
"Citizens won't believe in a Europe which doesn't give them tangible benefits," Italian Union for Europe deputy Roberto Mezzaroma told Lamfalussy during a debate on the EMI's annual report for 1996.
"People's well-being depends on jobs," he said.

From the other side of the political divide British Socialist Alan Donnelly reminded Lamfalussy of his prediction several years ago that it would be difficult to complete EMU unless unemployment was reduced.

Since then jobless figures had risen even further, Donnelly said, urging the EMI and the European Commission to recognise the change in mood in Europe, where nine of the 15 governments now hail from the centre-left, and balance the drive towards the single currency with a more concerted effort on jobs.
Parliament told Lamfalussy the EMI report's analysis of European Union unemployment problems was fundamentally flawed.

The EMI blamed continuing high unemployment on 'structural rigidities in labour markets', like minimum wages and social protection, but ignored other structural causes like low levels of research and investment and poor education systems, parliament said in a report drafted by Mezzaroma.

The modest economic recovery which the EU saw last year "has not brought about a substantial reduction in unemployment", essentially because "the bulk of EU unemployment appears to be of a structural rather than a cyclical nature", parliament said.

Improving public finances might have an impact on the cyclical causes but there would only be a sustained drop in unemployment if growth was accompanied by such measures as wage moderation, a more flexible labour market, cuts in the tax burden on companies, better education and training and investments in transport and communications infrastructure.

Responding to Euro-MPs' complaints, Lamfalussy agreed that while monetary policy might help reduce unemployment that was linked to feeble economic growth, with the aid of sensible budgetary policies, it could not affect job losses caused by structural factors.
But he stuck to his original script for remedies.

"I think that attacking...that part of unemployment that is not a result of growth weakness means the implementation of other policies, which are structural, which involve flexibility on the labour market and policies which will bear on indirect costs of employment," the Belgian EMI chief said.

The parliament generally welcomed the EMI's analysis of Europe's economic, monetary and financial progress as a useful tool for assessing the degree of economic convergence between member states and the state of preparations for the introduction of the EU single currency, the euro.
But they criticised the fledgling European Central Bank for skirting round the problems posed by the lack of coordination between national taxation policies.

In a second report, drafted by French Christian Democrat Andre Fourcans, the parliament warned that if national governments continued to have widely different taxation rates once a single currency is in place, there would be a grave risk of economic distortions.

"Unfair competition through tax and 'social dumping'...could be damaging for the member states that might be the victims in economic and social terms (relocalisation of activities, unemployment, dwindling tax revenue) but also disastrous in terms of political relations within the Union," parliament said.
Euro-MPs urged the member states to agree to a minimum degree of tax harmonisation, particularly for taxes on savings, businesses and cross-border transfers.

Decisions on indirect taxation should be taken on the basis of qualified majority voting, not unanimity, Euro-MPs said in a third report on a common EU system of VAT, prepared by German Socialist Christa Randzio-Plath.
